2026-10-24 / Project Confluence / Development note

Project Confluence — Developing the First Modular Facade Assets

Developing the first facade modules in Blender, testing them in Unreal Engine 5, and using architectural context to guide a second set of window and full-height opening variations.

Move from blockout to individual assets

After the spline infrastructure prototype, I shifted toward modular architecture. The aim was to begin producing architectural elements that could be evaluated in Confluence’s environment, bringing asset creation into the development process early.

The first set consisted of a plain wall, a wall with a window opening, and a separate window frame. Working with a limited set kept the focus on modeling, UV preparation, and the transfer from Blender to Unreal before expanding the range of components.

Establish the first Blender-to-Unreal pass

Preparing the initial assets involved working through wall openings, frame geometry, UVs, modifiers, and object origins. The first set was then exported from Blender and imported into Unreal Engine 5.

In the initial engine test, the opening passed through the wall correctly, while the applied PBR material and texture scale appeared reasonable. This provided a working starting point for evaluating the assets inside the environment.

The important step was moving beyond an isolated model. Once the components were placed in an architectural arrangement, their proportions could be judged against the surrounding facade and balcony.

Separate module size from opening size

The test supported keeping a 2-meter wall module as the base unit. A 4-meter balcony frontage could accommodate two units, providing space for a window and a full-height opening alongside each other.

The initial 1.2 × 1.4-meter window appeared suitable for a side facade, but felt small on the balcony-facing elevation. This was less apparent at a medium viewing distance and more noticeable close up.

Rather than changing the entire wall module, I kept its width and developed alternative openings. The module establishes the assembly rhythm; the opening proportions respond to the particular facade condition.

Build the next opening variations

The next modeling pass added two opening sizes: 1.6 × 1.5 meters and 1.6 × 2.3 meters. Each variation included a matching wall, separate frame, and glass geometry, with UV preparation completed in Blender.

The new frames also received a 45-degree angle-based smoothing treatment. This made shading preparation part of the asset workflow alongside geometry and UVs.

The larger window and full-height opening were then imported into Unreal and assembled into the balcony facade. Comparing the smaller and larger window in substantially the same view made the change in facade proportions easier to assess. They remain simple architectural components at this stage, without detailed opening mechanisms or hardware.

To keep the growing set easy to navigate, I retained “Window” in the asset naming and used dimensions to distinguish the variations.

Supporting evidence / Window-frame UVs

What this stage establishes

This session produced an initial facade asset set, a first Blender-to-Unreal import test, and a second modeling and in-engine assembly pass informed by the proportions observed in the environment.

It is still an early building kit. The work does not yet establish a complete residential building, a finished retrofit system, or a kit validated across the entire district. Glass geometry is part of the set, while its final in-engine appearance remains a separate material task.

The most useful lesson was to evaluate assets in context before expanding them. The first import made the components available in Unreal; the facade test gave the next modeling pass a concrete direction.
